Let’s take SDG 3 (Good Health & Well-being) as an example.
Here’s how the calculation works step by step:
Step 1 – Raw Data: Actual values like 103, 34, and 85% (from surveys/statistics).
Step 2 – Target: 2030 goal values (like MMR = 70, Immunization = 100%).
Step 3 – Normalization: Convert each into a score between 0–100 (closer to target →  
higher score).
Step 4 – Goal Score: Average all three indicator scores = (72 + 74 + 85) / 3 = 77.
Step 5 – Composite Index: Combine with other SDGs to get India’s final SDG Index.
So, the raw numbers (103, 34, 85%) are the starting point, and through normalization + 
averaging, they become a single comparable score out of 100.

What will make the SDGs successful 
1.Strong Political Will 
– Governments must commit to long-term 
implementation beyond short-term politics.
2.Adequate Financing 
 – Mobilizing global and local resources, 
including public, private, and innovative funding.
3.Partnerships 
 – Collaboration among governments, civil society, 
businesses, and international organizations.
4.Inclusive Approach 
 – Ensuring no one is left behind, especially 
marginalized and vulnerable groups.
5.Reliable Data & Monitoring 
 – Robust indicators and transparent 
reporting to track progress.
6.Integration 
– Aligning economic growth, social inclusion, and 
environmental protection in national policies.

Here are a few examples of new companies that are developing in the
sustainability sector in the US, Europe, and Asia, along with the SDGs
that they are committed to achieving:
1.Tesla (US): Tesla is committed to achieving several of the SDGs,
including SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy) and SDG 13 (Climate
Action). The company produces electric vehicles and solar panels to help
reduce greenhouse gas emissions and promote clean energy.
2.Unilever (Europe): Unilever is committed to achieving several of the
SDGs, including SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being) and SDG 12
(Responsible Consumption and Production). The company produces a
range of consumer goods, including food, personal care, and cleaning
products, and has committed to reducing its environmental impact and
promoting sustainable consumption.

4. BYD (Asia): BYD is committed to achieving several of the SDGs,
including SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities) and SDG 13
(Climate Action). The company produces electric buses, cars, and
other vehicles, and also provides renewable energy solutions such as
solar panels and energy storage systems.
5.Grameen Bank (Asia): Grameen Bank is committed to achieving
several of the SDGs, including SDG 1 (No Poverty) and SDG 5
(Gender Equality). The bank provides microfinance loans to people
living in poverty, particularly women, to help them start businesses
and improve their livelihoods.
6.Patagonia (US): Patagonia is committed to achieving several of the
SDGs, including SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production)
and SDG 14 (Life Below Water). The company produces outdoor

Study finds some UN SDGs could damage forests, some others may 
be beneficial
•SDG Trade-offs: While SDGs aim to balance environment and
development, some energy (SDG 7) and infrastructure (SDG 9) targets
risk harming forests.
•Renewable
Energy
Expansion:
Large-scale
solar,
wind,
and
hydropower projects often require clearing land and forest areas,
reducing biodiversity.
•Infrastructure Growth: Roads, railways, and transmission lines
fragment habitats, opening forests to logging, mining, and poaching.
•Hydropower
Concerns:
Dam
construction
can
flood
forest
ecosystems, displace communities, and disrupt river ecology.
•Forest Dependency: Indigenous and forest-dependent communities
are most affected, losing livelihoods and cultural ties.
